anatomy.intro: Fleshy leaves, spiny cushions, and cylindrical branches give Eve's needle its unusually leafy outline.

parts.function: A fleshy, pointed leaf adds photosynthetic surface to young growth.
parts.label: Awl-shaped leaf

parts.function: This specialized cactus growth point bears the spines beside the leaf.
parts.label: Areole

parts.function: The sharp spine protects the soft, water-storing tissues.
parts.label: Spine

parts.function: The green stem stores water and supports successive branches.
parts.label: Cylindrical stem

flowers.text: Tubular flowers reach about 2–3 inches long, in yellow-green, orange-red, or red. Container-grown plants rarely bloom.

growth.note: Older stems develop dark brown bark and a woody trunk beneath the younger green branches.

stages.text: New stem growth carries soft-looking pointed leaves.
stages.title: Leafy tip

stages.text: Side shoots extend the upright framework.
stages.title: Branching shrub

stages.text: Older plants develop a stronger trunk beneath the succulent branches.
stages.title: Woody base

habitat.text: Eve's needle comes from the Peruvian Andes. Its branching, spiny framework provides shelter for small animals and birds, while its roots help stabilize soil in dry landscapes.

No flowers, grafts, or roots. Numbers must remain readable at 350px. Generic anatomical specimen, not measurement evidence. Eve's needle cactus: small upright branching green cylindrical cactus stems with knobby tubercles, sparse pale areoles, sharp ivory spines, and conspicuous long narrow succulent awl-shaped leaves on young upper growth. 1 points to an awl-shaped fleshy leaf; 2 to a pale areole at a leaf base; 3 to an ivory spine; 4 to the green cylindrical main stem. Leaves must be distinct from spines.

lookalikes.name: Paper spine cactus
lookalikes.text: Paper spine builds stacks of short detachable segments with flat, papery spines; Eve's needle has leafy, cylindrical branches.

mature.text: In habitat it can reach roughly 13 ft (4 m), with a trunk up to 4 inches across; plants in cultivation usually stay much smaller.

nameStory.text: The epithet subulata refers to an awl shape: the long pointed leaves provide the clue to the name.
